## Regression and the Linear Model

Given observations $(y_i,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ip})$, $i=1,\dots,n$, of a scalar
**response** (dependent variable) $y$ and **covariates** (explanatory
variables) $x=(x_1,\dots,x_p)$, [[regression-analysis]] studies the
**conditional expectation function**

$$
\mu(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
$$

This function can have any shape, so it cannot be estimated without further
assumptions. **Linear regression** assumes that $\mu$ is affine in $x$,

$$
\mu(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots+\beta_px_p,
$$

which allows closed-form parameter estimates by **ordinary least squares
(OLS)**, see [[least-squares-estimation]]. With $p=1$ it is called **simple
linear regression** (SLR), and with $p>1$ **multiple linear regression**
(MLR). Both differ from **multivariate linear regression**, where several
correlated responses are predicted. Regression models the conditional
distribution of the response given the covariates rather than the joint
distribution of all variables, which is the subject of multivariate analysis.

## The Model

For each statistical unit $i=1,\dots,n$,

$$
y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\dots+\beta_px_{ip}+\varepsilon_i
=\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}+\varepsilon_i,
$$

where $\beta_0$ is the **intercept**, $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_p$ are the
**slopes** (the effect on $\mu$ of a unit change in $x_j$, other covariates
held fixed) and $\varepsilon_i$ is the **error term** that adds noise to the
relationship. In matrix form

$$
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{y}=\begin{bmatrix}y_1\\\vdots\\y_n\end{bmatrix},\quad
\mathbf{X}=\begin{bmatrix}1&x_{11}&\cdots&x_{1p}\\
\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&\cdots&x_{np}\end{bmatrix},\quad
\boldsymbol{\beta}=\begin{bmatrix}\beta_0\\\vdots\\\beta_p\end{bmatrix},\quad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}=\begin{bmatrix}\varepsilon_1\\\vdots\\\varepsilon_n
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The standard assumptions are

1. **Linearity** and **weak exogeneity**: $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X]=0$,
2. **Constant variance** (homoscedasticity): $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2$,
3. **Independence** (or uncorrelatedness) of the errors,
4. **No perfect multicollinearity**: $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank.

For exact finite-sample inference one also assumes
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I_n)$, see
[[normal-distribution]].

## Simple Linear Regression

For $p=1$ the model is $y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i$.

:::{.definition data-title="OLS Estimators"}

The **ordinary least squares** estimators minimise the residual sum of
squares

$$
\mathrm{RSS}(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2.
$$

:::

Setting the partial derivatives to zero gives the **normal equations**

$$
\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0,\qquad
\sum_ix_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0,
$$

with solution

$$
\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}
=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x,
$$

where $\bar x,\bar y$ are the sample means. The fitted line passes through
$(\bar x,\bar y)$, and the slope is the sample covariance of $x,y$ over the
sample variance of $x$.

## OLS in General

For general $p$, minimising
$\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta\|^2$ and
setting the gradient $-2\mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta)$
to zero gives the normal equations $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta=
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$, hence

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}.
$$

The matrix $\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}$ is invertible exactly when there is no
perfect multicollinearity. Geometrically, the fitted values
$\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{X}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=H\mathbf{y}$ with
$H=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$ are the
orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space of $\mathbf{X}$
(see [[orthogonality-and-projections]]), and the residuals
$\hat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ are orthogonal to
every column of $\mathbf{X}$. An unbiased estimator of the error variance is

$$
\hat\sigma^2=\frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{n-p-1}.
$$

## Properties of the Estimators

:::{.theorem data-title="Gauss-Markov"}

Under assumptions 1-4, $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is unbiased,
$\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$, with covariance matrix

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1},
$$

and it has the smallest covariance among all linear unbiased estimators
(it is the **BLUE**).

:::

:::{.proof}

Since $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\boldsymbol\beta+(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}
\mathbf{X}^\top\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, taking expectations gives unbiasedness
and taking covariances gives the variance formula. For another linear
unbiased estimator $\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}=C\mathbf{y}$ write
$C=(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top+D$. Unbiasedness forces
$D\mathbf{X}=0$, so
$\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})=\sigma^2CC^\top
=\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}+\sigma^2DD^\top$, and $DD^\top$ is
positive semi-definite.

:::

For SLR this gives

$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}},\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\sigma^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\right).
$$

If in addition the errors are normal, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\sim
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1})$ (it is
also the maximum likelihood estimator), and
$(n-p-1)\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-p-1}$ independently of
$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. Each standardised coefficient
$(\hat\beta_j-\beta_j)/\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\beta_j)$ then follows a
[[students-t-distribution|Student $t$ distribution]] with $n-p-1$ degrees of
freedom, giving confidence intervals and tests, and joint hypotheses use the
[[f-distribution]].

## Multiple Regression: Categorical Predictors and Interactions

In MLR each slope $\beta_j$ is interpreted holding the other covariates
fixed, which is why correlated covariates make estimates unstable (large
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_j)$).

**Dummy variables.** A categorical covariate with $L$ levels is encoded by
$L-1$ indicator variables $d_\ell=\mathbb{1}\{\text{level}=\ell\}$, with one
level kept as the baseline. Using all $L$ indicators together with an
intercept would give perfect multicollinearity. The coefficient on $d_\ell$ is
the shift in the mean response relative to the baseline level.

**Interaction terms.** To let the effect of one covariate depend on another,
add their product,

$$
y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_3x_1x_2+\varepsilon,
$$

so that the slope in $x_1$ is $\beta_1+\beta_3x_2$. Interacting a dummy with a
continuous covariate gives a separate slope for each category.

:::{.example data-title="Fitting a Regression"}

Simulate $y=1+2x+\varepsilon$ and recover the coefficients with OLS.

::: {#00df2086 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 200)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 1, 200)
fit = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
print(fit.params)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
[1.04711649 1.97469853]
```
:::
:::


Residual diagnostics (residuals against fitted values, normal Q-Q plot)
check the constant variance, linearity and normality assumptions.

:::

Choosing which covariates to include is the subject of [[model-selection]].
Responses that are binary or counts require the generalisation to the
[[glm]], for instance [[logistic-regression]] and [[poisson-regression]].
